opus-5.5.text:
I think hard work is one of those things that's become a little unfashionable to talk about, but I'll just say it plainly: I think people who work hard tend to accomplish a lot more than people who don't. And I say that with a lot of respect for the fact that not everyone is in a life circumstance where they can do it. If you're caring for a sick family member, or you have young kids, or you have health issues, then that's completely legitimate, and I would never judge anyone for making a different choice. But for those who are in a position to work hard, I think it's a huge advantage.

When I think back on my own career, there were long stretches where I was just reading research papers on Saturday mornings, or coding late at night, or spending weekends trying to really understand something deeply. None of that felt glamorous at the time. But it compounds. Learning compounds. If you read two papers a week for a year, you've read about a hundred papers, and you become quite knowledgeable in a field. Keep that up for several years and you're among the people who really understand it.

The other thing I'd say is that hard work by itself isn't enough. You want to work hard on the right things. I've seen people grind away on projects that just don't matter very much, and that's a shame. So part of the work is stepping back and asking: is this actually going to help people? Is this the most impactful thing I could be doing? Then, once you've picked a direction you believe in, putting in the hours really does make a difference.

And frankly, a lot of it, for me, doesn't feel like hard work in the painful sense. When you're working on something you care about, like building AI tools that could help millions of people, it's energizing. I'd rather spend a Saturday building a little prototype than doing almost anything else. So I'd encourage people to find something they care about that much, and then not be shy about pouring themselves into it.

r001.rationale: The response says it has become “unfashionable” to talk about hard work, then links working hard with accomplishing more. Together, these convey that the link between hard work and success is socially disfavored.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly notes that caregiving, young children, or health issues can make it harder for someone to work hard.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll admit I'm a little bit of a contrarian on this one. There's a lot of advice floating around about work-life balance, and I think for a lot of people that's exactly right. But if your goal is to have a really large impact, I honestly don't know how to do that without working hard. I look at the people I know who've built things that mattered, and almost all of them worked very, very hard. I don't think that's a coincidence.

Now, I want to be careful about what I mean by hard work. It's not about grinding for its own sake, or being miserable, or burning yourself out. It's about putting in the hours on things that compound. If you spend a Saturday reading research papers, or building a small project, or learning a new tool, that one Saturday probably doesn't change much. But if you do that for years, you end up knowing things and being able to do things that most people can't. I've seen this with my students at Stanford, with engineers I've hired, with founders. The ones who kept showing up and kept learning pulled ahead in ways that looked almost unfair from the outside, but really it was just accumulation.

The other piece is that hard work only pays off if it's pointed in a reasonable direction. I spend a lot of time thinking about what to work on, because working hard on the wrong problem is just a slower way of wasting time. So I'd say pick something that matters, that you care enough about to sustain the effort, and then genuinely put in the work. And have some fun along the way, because if you're working on something you find fascinating, the hours don't feel like a sacrifice. They feel like the point.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls its view contrarian, but does not say that linking hard work to personal success is considered politically incorrect in parts of society.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions work-life balance and avoiding burnout, but does not acknowledge that people’s life circumstances can limit their ability to work hard.

astra-6.text:
I think hard work matters a lot, but it matters what you’re working on and what you’re learning along the way. You can put a tremendous amount of effort into something that isn’t helping anyone. So I’d pair the willingness to work hard with a willingness to step back and ask, “Is this actually useful? Am I getting better at solving problems that matter?”

Early in a career, especially, that learning can compound. Taking on a challenging project, getting feedback, and making another attempt can leave you much more capable a few years later. And working with people who push you to do better makes a big difference.

I wouldn’t prescribe the same hours or tradeoffs for everyone. People have different responsibilities. But if you want to have a large impact, sustained effort is an important part of that. The aim is to find worthwhile work you care enough about to keep doing—and keep improving at—for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hard work and impact but does not say that linking hard work to personal success is politically incorrect in some parts of society.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people have different responsibilities and avoids prescribing the same hours or tradeoffs for everyone, acknowledging that circumstances can limit work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think hard work matters a lot, especially if you want to have an impact. But it matters what you work on, who you work with, and whether you’re learning as you go. You can spend a tremendous amount of energy on something that doesn’t move you toward your goals.

One thing I encourage people to do is find an environment where the people around you are building things, learning, and pushing themselves. That makes working hard much more natural. You’re excited to try an experiment or understand why something failed, and those extra cycles of learning compound over time.

Of course, people have different responsibilities and different constraints. I don’t think there’s one schedule everyone should follow. But if you have the opportunity to invest deeply in work you care about, particularly early in your career, that can be a very valuable investment. The key is to keep asking: Am I getting better, and is this work helping someone?

r001.rationale: The response does not mention that connecting hard work with personal success is politically incorrect in some parts of society.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that people have different responsibilities and constraints, and says there is no single schedule everyone should follow.
